title: Model Optimization & Your Personal Copilot System

sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

This is the capstone lesson for Copilot mastery. By now you know every major Copilot feature. This lesson is about pulling it all together into a personal optimization system — deliberate choices about which model, which mode, and which tools to use for each type of task.

The developers who get the most from Copilot aren't the ones who use it most — they're the ones who use it most deliberately. They know which model to reach for, which mode is right for the situation, and when NOT to use AI at all.

You'll learn:
- The current model landscape and what each model is actually best for
- The Mode Selection Framework: Ask vs. Edit vs. Agent vs. CLI
- How to benchmark models on your own work
- Building a personal optimization document that evolves with the tooling
- Knowing when to step away from AI assistance

## The Current Model Landscape (2025-2026)

Model availability changes frequently. The key is to understand the categories, not memorize specific model names.

### Auto Mode — The Smart Default

Copilot has an **Auto** model option that selects the best model for each request automatically, based on the task type and current availability. For most day-to-day tasks, Auto is the right choice — it reduces cognitive overhead and stays current as models are updated.

When to use Auto: routine coding, quick questions, chat interactions where speed matters more than maximum quality.

### When to Switch Manually

**OpenAI Models (GPT-4.1, GPT-4o, GPT-5 family)**
- General coding tasks across any language
- Reliable, consistent performance
- GPT-4.1 is included with subscription (no premium request cost)
- GPT-5 family provides significantly stronger reasoning at premium request cost

**Reasoning Models (o3, o4-mini, GPT-5 with extended thinking)**
- Complex debugging where the bug isn't obvious
- Algorithm design and optimization
- Code that involves non-trivial logic (complex state machines, mathematical algorithms)
- Multi-step problems where the default model gives a shallow answer
- Slower but notably more thorough — use when quality matters more than speed

**Claude Models (Sonnet, Opus — Anthropic)**
- Professional writing: documentation, reports, PR descriptions, commit messages
- Complex explanations for non-technical audiences
- Long document analysis and summarization
- Nuanced code review comments
- Working with large context windows (1M token context available on some Claude models)
- When you want the most readable, clearly structured prose output

**Gemini Models (Flash, Pro — Google)**
- Fast, iterative interactions where response speed matters
- When rate-limited on other models
- Multimodal tasks (image + code analysis)
- Gemini Pro for complex analysis tasks

**MAI-Code-1-Flash (Microsoft)**
- Microsoft first-party model
- Continuously improving — good to benchmark periodically
- Zero latency advantage for Azure-hosted workloads

**Extended Context Models**
Some models (especially Claude) support 1 million token context. Use this for:
- Working with very large codebases where you need to include many files
- Analyzing long documents (lengthy policy documents, full audit logs)
- Multi-file refactors where you need to maintain context across many files simultaneously

## The Mode Selection Framework

Copilot has four main operating modes. Using the wrong mode for a task wastes time — the right mode gets you to the answer faster with less back-and-forth.

### Mode Decision Tree

**Question: What do you need?**

**ANSWER/EXPLAIN → Use Ask Mode (Copilot Chat)**
- You want an answer, explanation, or analysis
- You're exploring options before deciding
- You want to understand something about your code or a concept
- Best models: Auto, Claude for explanations, reasoning model for complex analysis

**CHANGE SPECIFIC FILES → Use Edit Mode**
- You know which files need to change
- You want to review every diff before accepting
- The change is well-defined (not exploratory)
- You have 3-20 files in scope
- Best models: Auto or GPT-4.1 for code changes, Claude for changes that require writing

**AUTONOMOUS MULTI-STEP TASK → Use Agent Mode**
- The task has multiple steps that can be delegated
- Copilot can determine which files to change
- You can supervise and approve at each step
- MCP tools give it the external data it needs
- Best models: Reasoning model (o3, o4-mini) for complex tasks, Auto for routine tasks

**TERMINAL-NATIVE WORK → Use CLI**
- You're working primarily in the terminal
- You want to delegate a long task in the background (`&` prefix)
- You want persistent memory across sessions
- You want session chronicles and standups
- Best models: select with `/model` in CLI

### Mode + Model Quick Reference

| Task | Mode | Model |
|------|------|-------|
| Explain this code | Ask | Claude Sonnet |
| Find a bug across files | Ask with @workspace | Reasoning (o3/o4) |
| Refactor 5 files | Edit | Auto / GPT-4.1 |
| Write PR description | Ask/CLI | Claude Sonnet |
| Add feature (multi-file) | Agent | Auto / Reasoning |
| Review PR for security | Ask or CLI /review | Claude or Reasoning |
| Quick code generation | Inline (ghost text) | (no choice — default) |
| Generate tests | Ask with /tests | Auto + manual prompting |
| Write documentation | Ask/Edit | Claude Opus |
| Database query via MCP | Agent | Auto |
| Background long task | CLI with & | Select with /model |

## When NOT to Use Copilot

The best developers using AI know when to set it aside. AI assistance actively hurts in some situations.

### Don't Use Copilot When:

**Learning something new for the first time.**
If you're learning a new language, framework, or algorithm, let yourself struggle. The struggle is the learning. Copilot completing code you don't understand builds technical debt in your brain — you can write the code but you can't fix it when it breaks.

**Making security-critical architecture decisions.**
Copilot gives you plausible-sounding answers. Security architecture decisions (authentication schemes, encryption choices, access control models) require human expertise and peer review, not AI suggestions. Use Copilot to implement decisions made by security experts, not to make the decisions.

**Code you don't understand.**
If Copilot generates code and you don't understand what it does, accepting it creates a maintenance problem. Rule: never accept code you can't explain. Ask Copilot to explain it first — if you still don't understand, don't accept it.

**Highly creative or novel design work.**
For genuinely novel system design — solving a problem no one has solved quite the same way before — the AI's training on existing patterns can constrain your thinking. Sketch the design yourself first, then use Copilot to implement it.

**When the context window is nearly full.**
If you've been working in the same long session and the model's context is heavily compacted, quality degrades. Start a fresh session for important new tasks rather than working with a degraded context.

### The 5-Minute Rule
If you've been going back and forth with Copilot for more than 5 minutes on one problem and the quality isn't improving, stop and do it manually. Some problems are better solved by thinking than by prompting.

## Benchmarking Models on Your Own Work

Generic model comparisons are useful context, but your specific work may respond differently. Benchmark models on your actual tasks.

### 3-Task Benchmarking Protocol

Choose 3 representative tasks from your work — one for each model category you're considering. Run each task on 2-3 models and score the output.

**Scoring dimensions:**
1. Correctness (0-3): Is the output factually and functionally correct?
2. Completeness (0-3): Does it cover everything needed without over-generating?
3. Usability (0-3): How much editing is needed before it's usable?
4. Speed (0-3): Was the response time acceptable for this task?

**Score 12 total. Highest score wins for that task type.**

### Tracking Your Results

Keep a simple log of your benchmarks. After 10-15 benchmark runs, you'll have strong personal evidence for which models serve your specific work best. This evidence is more valuable than any generic model comparison.

### When to Re-Benchmark

Models are updated continuously. Re-benchmark:
- When a new model version is announced
- When you notice quality degradation in a model you rely on
- When a new model type becomes available (e.g., when a new reasoning model drops)
- Quarterly as a standard practice

**The BYOK option (Bring Your Own Key).** Copilot supports connecting your own API keys for models you've subscribed to directly. If you have an Anthropic API key with access to Opus 4.8 or another model not in the standard Copilot selection, you can connect it via the model picker → 'Add custom model'. This gives you access to the full range of models from each provider, beyond what Copilot bundles. Useful for specialized work where the bundled model selection doesn't include the model you want.

sections.title: Build Your Personal Copilot Optimization Document
sections.content:
Create a living optimization document that will guide your Copilot usage and evolve with your experience.

**Create `COPILOT-MY-SETUP.md`** in your home directory or personal notes folder. This is for you, not your team.

**Section 1 — My Current Configuration**
- Copilot plan: [Individual/Business/Enterprise]
- VS Code version: [check in Help → About]
- Custom instructions file: [path — does it exist?]
- MCP servers configured: [list with purpose]
- Prompt files created: [list with purpose]
- Agent skills installed: [list with purpose]

**Section 2 — My Model Preferences (update after benchmarking)**
```
For code generation: [model] because [reason]
For documentation/writing: [model] because [reason]
For complex debugging: [model] because [reason]
For quick questions: [model] because [reason]
For agent tasks: [model] because [reason]
```

**Section 3 — My Mode Selection Rules**
Fill in with your own judgment after the lessons:
```
I use Ask mode when: ...
I use Edit mode when: ...
I use Agent mode when: ...
I use CLI when: ...
I DON'T use Copilot when: ...
```

**Section 4 — My Custom Instructions Summary**
Key rules from your copilot-instructions.md explained in plain English — what each rule does and why you added it.

**Section 5 — Experiments in Progress**
Things you're currently testing or trying to improve.

**Section 6 — What I've Learned Doesn't Work**
Specific patterns or prompts you've tried that consistently produce bad results. This section saves you from repeating mistakes.

**Date this document.** Update it monthly — or whenever you discover something significant about your Copilot usage.

sections.title: Workshop A — Run Your 3-Task Benchmark
sections.content:
Benchmark 3 models on 3 tasks representative of your actual work.

**Choose 3 tasks from different categories:**
- Task 1: A code generation task (write a function, implement a feature)
- Task 2: A writing task (documentation, PR description, explanation)
- Task 3: An analysis task (explain complex code, find a bug, review for issues)

**For each task, run it on 3 models:**
Use the model picker in Copilot Chat to switch. Give each model the identical prompt.

**Score each model (0-3 per dimension):**

| Task | Model | Correct | Complete | Usable | Speed | Total |
|------|-------|---------|----------|--------|-------|-------|
| Task 1 | GPT-4.1 | | | | | |
| Task 1 | Claude Sonnet | | | | | |
| Task 1 | [Third model] | | | | | |
| Task 2 | GPT-4.1 | | | | | |
| Task 2 | Claude Sonnet | | | | | |
| Task 2 | [Third model] | | | | | |
| Task 3 | GPT-4.1 | | | | | |
| Task 3 | Claude Sonnet | | | | | |
| Task 3 | [Third model] | | | | | |

**Analyze your results:**
- Which model won for code generation?
- Which model won for writing?
- Which model won for analysis?
- Were the differences significant or marginal?

**Update Section 2 of your optimization document** with your personal benchmark findings.

**Most important outcome:** Your model preferences are now based on evidence from your specific work, not generic internet comparisons.

sections.title: Workshop B — The Full Workflow Integration
sections.content:
Take a real work task from start to finish using the optimal Copilot tool at each step.

**Choose a real task** that spans multiple activities. Example: add a new feature, fix a reported bug, or process a new data source.

**Step 1 — Understand the task (Ask Mode + @workspace)**
```
@workspace Explain what I would need to change to [your task]. 
What files are involved? What's the dependency chain?
Model: Claude Sonnet (understanding and explanation)
```

**Step 2 — Plan the implementation (Agent Mode or Ask + reasoning model)**
```
Outline the implementation plan. What should I change first, second, third?
Are there any risks or edge cases I should consider before starting?
Model: o3 or o4-mini (reasoning task)
```

**Step 3 — Implement (Edit Mode or Agent Mode)**
For 2-5 files: Edit Mode, model: Auto.
For 6+ files or autonomous tasks: Agent Mode, model: Auto or reasoning.
Review every diff before accepting.

**Step 4 — Write tests (Ask Mode with /tests + edge case prompting)**
```
/tests #file:[changed-file]
Focus on: [specific scenarios from step 2's risk analysis]
Model: Auto
```

**Step 5 — Documentation (Ask Mode)**
```
Update the documentation for the changes in #file:[changed-file].
Model: Claude Sonnet
```

**Step 6 — Commit message (CLI or Ask)**
```
Write a conventional commits message for these changes.
Explain the why, not just the what.
Model: Claude Sonnet
```

**Step 7 — PR description (Ask or CLI)**
Model: Claude Sonnet

**Debrief:** Which step benefited most from AI assistance? Which step needed the most correction? Where would you have gotten the same result faster without AI?

sections.title: Workshop C — Copilot Mastery Review
sections.content:
A final capstone review across everything you've learned in the Copilot lessons.

**Create a `COPILOT-MASTERY-CHECKLIST.md`** — an honest assessment of your current level.

**For each capability, mark: Confident / Learning / Not Yet Used**

**Core Copilot:**
- [ ] Ghost text partial acceptance (Ctrl+→)
- [ ] Next Edit Suggestions navigation
- [ ] Comment-first technique for generation
- [ ] Anchor pattern for repetitive code

**Copilot Chat:**
- [ ] @workspace for cross-file questions
- [ ] @terminal for terminal error diagnosis
- [ ] @github for repository search
- [ ] #file and #selection variable attachment
- [ ] /explain, /fix, /doc, /tests slash commands
- [ ] Combining participants, variables, and slash commands

**Copilot Edits:**
- [ ] Building a working set of files
- [ ] Writing precise multi-file instructions
- [ ] Hunk-level accept/reject
- [ ] Iterative refinement in one session

**Custom Configuration:**
- [ ] copilot-instructions.md created for a real project
- [ ] Path-specific instruction files
- [ ] At least one .prompt.md file

**GitHub Copilot CLI:**
- [ ] Installed and authenticated
- [ ] /diff and /review commands used
- [ ] /chronicle standup run
- [ ] Background delegation with &

**PR and Code Review:**
- [ ] PR description generated
- [ ] Copilot review requested on a real PR
- [ ] At least one suggestion applied with one click

**MCP and Integrations:**
- [ ] At least one MCP server configured
- [ ] Jira or ADO connected and tested
- [ ] Multi-server setup with env var references

**Security and Governance:**
- [ ] Content exclusions configured for sensitive files
- [ ] Security review prompt used on generated code
- [ ] Data protection level for my plan understood

**Model Selection:**
- [ ] Benchmark completed on my own tasks
- [ ] Personal model selection rules documented
- [ ] Claude used for writing tasks
- [ ] Reasoning model used for complex analysis

**For every item marked 'Not Yet Used':** Schedule it for this week. Don't let the knowledge from this lesson series go untested.

**Outcome:** A honest, actionable picture of your current Copilot mastery — and a clear path to fill the remaining gaps.

sections.question: A colleague says they always use the reasoning model (o3) for every Copilot task because it's the most powerful. Is this optimal?
options: Yes — always use the best model available for every task

No — reasoning models are slower and use more premium credits. For routine tasks (quick code completion, simple chat questions), the speed and cost penalty outweighs the quality difference. Use reasoning models for tasks that genuinely require deeper reasoning.
It depends on your subscription tier
No — reasoning models should only be used in Agent Mode
sections.explanation: Reasoning models (o3, o4-mini, o3-pro, etc.) are genuinely more capable for complex reasoning tasks — but they're also slower and consume more premium request credits. For routine tasks like explaining a function, generating a simple utility, or quick chat questions, the default model (GPT-4.1) or Auto provides the same quality at a fraction of the time and cost. Use reasoning models deliberately: for complex debugging, non-trivial algorithm design, and multi-step analysis where the reasoning depth is observable. For everything else, let Auto choose or use the standard model.

sections.question: You've been in the same Copilot CLI session for 3 hours, working on a complex debugging task. You now want to start a completely different, unrelated task. What should you do for best results?
options: Continue in the same session — Copilot remembers everything from the last 3 hours
Run /compact, then start the new task in the same session
Start a new CLI session or run /compact and recognize that the previous 3 hours of context has been summarized and the new task has maximum fresh context
Close the terminal and reopen it to clear all state
sections.explanation: After 3 hours, the context window may have been compacted multiple times. Running /compact summarizes what remains, but the detailed context from early in the session is gone. For a completely new, unrelated task, you can either: (1) start a completely new CLI session to give the new task a clean, full context window, or (2) run /compact and start the new task in the current session, which gives maximum remaining context. The previous session's detailed work is summarized, not fully preserved. If the old task context is not relevant to the new task, a new session is cleaner.

sections.content: **Lesson 6-22 complete — and the core GitHub Copilot track is done.** You've now covered GitHub Copilot from first suggestion to enterprise governance: 17 lessons covering ghost text, chat participants, edits, agent mode, custom instructions, prompt files, CLI, PR review, extensions, MCP, testing, documentation, security, team governance, and model optimization. The student who completes all 17 of these lessons with hands-on practice will be in the top 1% of Copilot users — not because they know more features, but because they use every feature deliberately. Part 11 continues with lesson 6-23: applying Copilot beyond code, starting with email and inbox management.
